title: Grade 7
emphasis: Abstract ideas and more precise argument

words.definition: fair to everyone; not favoring one side over another

hero.text: When Bolt and Pixel argued over whose plan to use, Juniper stayed impartial and judged both plans by the same rules.

words.everyday: A good referee stays impartial, even when her cousin is playing on one of the teams.

contrast.nonExample: The judge of the art contest gave first prize to her best friend's painting without looking closely at the others.
contrast.explanation: An impartial judge treats every side the same way. Favoring a friend is the opposite of impartial.

items.prompt: Which person is being impartial?

options.text: A debate judge who cheers whenever her own school's team speaks.
A teacher who grades every essay with the same rubric, without looking at names.
A coach who lets his son start every game.
A reporter who interviews only people who agree with her.

items.hint: Look for the person who treats every side the same way.
items.explanation: Impartial means not favoring anyone. Grading with the same rubric and hiding names keeps the teacher from playing favorites.

wrong.a: Cheering for her own school shows she favors one side.
wrong.c: Always starting his son is favoritism.
wrong.d: Hearing only one side is one-sided, not impartial.

items.prompt: The prefix im- means "not." Partial can mean "favoring one side." So impartial most likely means…
items.hint: Put "not" in front of "favoring one side."
items.explanation: Im- (not) + partial (favoring one side) = not favoring any side. "Partly finished" uses a different meaning of partial that doesn't fit here.

wrong.a: That is another meaning of partial (incomplete), but impartial is about fairness.
wrong.b: That is what partial means, without the "not."
wrong.d: An impartial person can decide; they just decide fairly.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The two towns had argued about the river for years. To settle it, they hired a mediator from far away, someone with no land, friends, or family in either town. They wanted someone truly ___.
items.clue: no land, friends, or family in either town
items.hint: Why would it matter that the person had no ties to either town?
items.explanation: Having no land, friends, or family in either town means the mediator has no reason to favor one side. That is impartial. Experienced might be nice, but the clue is about having no connections.

wrong.c: The passage stresses having no ties, not having skill.
wrong.d: The mediator came from far away, the opposite of local.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what impartial means.

chunks.text: scored the projects without seeing students' names.
gave extra points to their own students.

items.hint: Which ending keeps the judges from favoring anyone?
items.explanation: Hiding names stops judges from favoring students they know, which keeps them impartial. Giving extra points to their own students is bias.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "impartial" in this sentence?
items.passage: Historians try to write impartial accounts, describing what each side in a war believed instead of choosing heroes and villains.
items.hint: What do you call an account that picks a side?
items.explanation: Biased means leaning toward one side, the opposite of impartial. Neutral is a synonym, not an opposite. An account can be detailed or accurate and still be biased.

wrong.c: Neutral means nearly the same as impartial.

words.definition: doubting that something is true until you see good evidence

hero.text: Rex was skeptical when a stranger claimed his gadget could make anyone fly, so he asked to see it tested first.

words.everyday: Mara was skeptical of the ad promising that the cream would cure acne overnight.

contrast.nonExample: Theo believed the online rumor right away and shared it with everyone he knew.
contrast.explanation: A skeptical person questions a claim and wants proof. Believing something instantly is the opposite.

items.prompt: Is Dev being skeptical?
items.passage: A website said a new drink makes people grow two inches taller. Dev said, "I'd want to see a real study before I believe that."
items.hint: Does Dev believe the claim right away, or does he want evidence?
items.explanation: Yes. Dev doubts the claim and asks for evidence first. Being skeptical means not believing until there is good proof.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the scientists' reaction?
items.passage: When a lab announced it had built a machine that runs forever without fuel, most scientists did not call the claim impossible right away. They simply asked to see the data and wanted other labs to repeat the test.
items.clue: asked to see the data; wanted other labs to repeat the test
items.hint: They didn't reject it outright, and they didn't believe it either.
items.explanation: The scientists doubted the claim but stayed open, asking for data. That is skeptical. Dismissive would mean rejecting it without checking, which the passage says they did not do.

wrong.d: Dismissive means waving something away; these scientists wanted to check.
wrong.c: Amazed people would believe it; these wanted proof.
wrong.a: Nothing shows anger.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The candidate promised to lower taxes and build three new schools at the same time. Voters who remembered last year's broken promises were ___, wondering where the money would come from.
items.clue: remembered last year's broken promises; wondering where the money would come from
items.hint: How would you feel about a promise if the last ones were broken?
items.explanation: Remembering broken promises and wondering about the money shows the voters doubted the claim. That is skeptical.

wrong.b: Confident voters would believe the promise.
wrong.a: Grateful means thankful; they haven't received anything.

items.prompt: Which line uses "skeptical" correctly?

options.text: "I'm skeptical that this old map is real. The paper looks brand new."
"I'm skeptical about the trip, so I packed my bag a week early!"
"She was so skeptical that she believed every word he said."
"The skeptical puppy wagged its tail at everyone."

items.hint: Look for someone who doubts something and gives a reason.
items.explanation: The speaker doubts the map and points to evidence (new-looking paper). That is skeptical. Believing every word is the opposite.

wrong.b: Packing early shows excitement, not doubt.
wrong.c: Believing every word is trusting, not skeptical.
wrong.d: Wagging at everyone shows friendliness, not doubt.

items.prompt: What does "skeptical" mean in this passage?
items.passage: In 1912, Alfred Wegener argued that the continents had once been joined. Many geologists were skeptical; they asked what force could possibly move entire continents. Only decades later did new evidence change their minds.
items.clue: asked what force could possibly move entire continents; new evidence change their minds
items.hint: What finally changed the geologists' minds?
items.explanation: The geologists questioned the idea and changed their minds only when new evidence arrived. Skeptical means doubtful until shown proof.

wrong.a: They asked questions; nothing shows insults.
wrong.d: They did not agree at first.

words.definition: to say or show the opposite of something, so that both cannot be true

hero.text: Kai said the lab was empty all night, but the security video contradicted him: it showed someone sneaking in at midnight.

words.everyday: The new fossil evidence contradicted the old idea that the dinosaur had no feathers.

contrast.nonExample: Lin said it rained on Tuesday, and the weather report also showed rain on Tuesday.
contrast.explanation: To contradict, two statements must disagree. When the report matches what Lin said, it supports her instead.

items.prompt: Contra- means "against" and dict means "say." What does contradict most likely mean?

options.text: to say the opposite of something

items.hint: Combine "against" with "say."
items.explanation: Contra (against) + dict (say) = to say against, or say the opposite. You see dict in dictionary and predict too.

wrong.a: Saying again would be repeating, not going against.
wrong.c: That is closer to dictate.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In his report, Omar wrote that the Titanic sank in 1915. His own source, a museum website, ___ him: it clearly listed the date as 1912.
items.clue: clearly listed the date as 1912
items.hint: Do the two dates match or disagree?
items.explanation: Omar wrote 1915, but the source said 1912. The source says the opposite of what he wrote, so it contradicted him. Confirmed would mean it agreed.

wrong.c: Confirmed means agreed with; the dates don't match.
wrong.b: The source did not repeat his date.

items.prompt: Does the second statement contradict the first?
items.passage: First: "Our school has the most students in the district." Second: "Our school has more students than any other school in the district."
items.hint: Do the two sentences disagree, or say the same thing in different words?
items.explanation: No. Both statements mean the same thing, so they agree. To contradict, the statements must be opposite so that both cannot be true.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what contradict means.

chunks.text: The witness said the car was red,
by showing the same red car.

items.hint: To contradict, the photo has to show something different.
items.explanation: A blue car is the opposite of what the witness said, so the photo contradicts her. Showing the same red car would support her.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "contradicts" in this sentence?
items.passage: The mayor says the park is safe at night, but the police report contradicts her claim.
items.hint: What would the report do if it agreed with the mayor?
items.explanation: Supports means backs up a claim, the opposite of contradicts. Questions is weaker than contradicts but goes in the same direction.

wrong.c: Questioning a claim leans toward contradicting it, not the opposite.
wrong.a: Ignoring the claim is neither agreeing nor disagreeing.

words.definition: seeming reasonable and likely to be true

hero.text: Pixel's guess that the power outage came from the storm was plausible, since lightning had struck near the station.

words.everyday: "The bus was late" is a plausible excuse on a snowy morning.

contrast.nonExample: Jake told his teacher a dragon flew off with his homework.
contrast.explanation: A plausible explanation could reasonably be true. A dragon story is not believable at all.

items.prompt: Which explanation is the most plausible?
items.passage: The cookies on the counter are gone, and there are crumbs leading to the dog's bed.

options.text: Aliens beamed the cookies into space.
The cookies melted into the counter.
A tiny wizard turned them invisible.

items.hint: Which explanation could reasonably be true, given the crumbs?
items.explanation: Plausible means reasonable and likely. The crumbs lead to the dog's bed, so "the dog ate them" makes sense. The others are not believable.

wrong.a: That is not believable.
wrong.b: Cookies don't melt into counters.
wrong.d: Wizards are not a reasonable explanation.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the detective's view of the story?
items.passage: The suspect said he was at the library all afternoon. The detective thought this could be true, since the man had a library card and a stack of books, but she still planned to check the sign-in sheet.
items.clue: could be true; still planned to check
items.hint: The story seems reasonable, but she hasn't confirmed it yet.
items.explanation: The detective thinks the story is reasonable but not yet confirmed. Plausible means likely or believable. Proven and certain are too strong, since she still wants to check.

wrong.a: Proven goes too far; she still needs to check.
wrong.d: Certain is too strong for something she plans to double-check.
wrong.b: Ridiculous means not believable at all, but she thinks it could be true.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Early astronomers noticed that ships seemed to sink below the horizon hull-first. The idea of a round Earth seemed ___, because a curved surface would hide the bottom of a ship before the top.
items.clue: because a curved surface would hide the bottom of a ship before the top
items.hint: The sentence gives a reason the explanation makes sense.
items.explanation: The "because" clause explains why a round Earth makes sense of what sailors saw. A reasonable, believable explanation is plausible.

wrong.c: The explanation clears up the mystery rather than adding one.
wrong.d: The explanation helps, so it isn't useless.

items.prompt: Is this a plausible excuse?
items.passage: Asked why he missed soccer practice, Ian said, "I was building a rocket to visit Mars with my little sister."
items.hint: Could this reasonably be true?
items.explanation: No. A kid building a rocket to Mars is not believable. A plausible excuse is one that could reasonably be true, like a dentist appointment.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "plausible" in this sentence?
items.passage: The author makes the time-travel plot feel plausible by explaining the science step by step.
items.hint: Why would explaining the science step by step matter to readers?
items.explanation: Explaining the science makes readers think the plot could happen. Believable matches plausible. Scientific describes the method, not the effect on readers.

wrong.d: The science is how the author does it; plausible describes the result: it seems believable.
wrong.a: A plot can be exciting without being believable.

words.definition: an opponent or enemy; someone you compete or struggle against

hero.text: In the academy chess final, Nova faced her toughest adversary: Bolt, who had never lost a match.

words.everyday: The two senators were adversaries in the election but shook hands after the results came in.

contrast.nonExample: Rosa and her lab partner worked together to finish the experiment.
contrast.explanation: An adversary is on the opposite side. A lab partner is working with you, so she is an ally, not an adversary.

items.prompt: In which sentence is one person acting as an adversary?

options.text: Ella's coach helped her practice her serve.
In the debate, Mason argued against Priya's side.
Leo's teammate passed him the ball.

items.hint: An adversary is on the other side.
items.explanation: Mason argues against Priya, so he is her opponent, her adversary. A coach, teammate, and grandmother are all on Ella's or Leo's side.

wrong.a: A coach helps you, not opposes you.
wrong.c: A teammate is an ally.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: During the American Revolution, Britain and France had been enemies for decades. That long history helps explain why France chose to help the colonists against its old ___.
items.clue: enemies for decades; against
items.hint: What do you call a country you've been enemies with for a long time?
items.explanation: "Enemies for decades" tells you Britain was France's long-time opponent, its adversary. Neighbor is true on a map, but it misses the clue about being enemies.

wrong.d: The clue is about being enemies, not location.
wrong.a: Partners work together; these countries were enemies.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "adversary" in this sentence?
items.passage: In the courtroom, the two lawyers were adversaries, but outside they were old friends.
items.hint: What do you call someone who is on your side?
items.explanation: An ally is on your side, the opposite of an adversary. Rival is a synonym. A judge is neutral, not an ally.

wrong.b: A rival is nearly the same as an adversary.
wrong.c: A judge stays neutral; that isn't the opposite of opponent.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what adversary means.
items.hint: Whom would a player study before a match?
items.explanation: A player studies her opponent's serve to prepare, so "adversary" fits. A cheering teammate is on her side, not an adversary.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the snake in this passage?
items.passage: For the young mongoose, the cobra was a dangerous foe. The two circled each other, each waiting for the other to make the first mistake.
items.clue: dangerous foe; circled each other
items.hint: "Foe" is a clue. What are the two animals doing?
items.explanation: "Dangerous foe" and circling each other show the cobra is the mongoose's opponent, its adversary. Victim suggests the cobra is helpless, but it is dangerous.

wrong.c: A dangerous foe is not helpless.
wrong.a: A companion keeps you company; these animals are fighting.

words.definition: to make a problem, pain, or worry less severe

hero.text: Juniper planted trees along the hot street to alleviate the summer heat for the people who lived there.

words.everyday: An ice pack can alleviate the swelling from a sprained ankle.

contrast.nonExample: Wearing shoes that were too tight made Ari's blisters worse.
contrast.explanation: To alleviate is to make something less bad. Making blisters worse is the opposite.

items.prompt: Does this action alleviate the problem?
items.passage: The cafeteria line was so long that students had only five minutes to eat. The principal opened a second serving line, and the wait was cut in half.
items.hint: Did the problem get less severe?
items.explanation: Yes. Opening a second line made the long wait less severe. To alleviate means to ease or lessen a problem, even if it isn't completely gone.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: After the drought destroyed local crops, volunteers trucked in rice and clean water. The supplies did not end the crisis, but they helped ___ the families' hunger for several weeks.
items.clue: did not end the crisis, but they helped
items.hint: The supplies helped, but they didn't end the problem.
items.explanation: "Did not end the crisis, but they helped" shows the hunger became less severe but did not disappear. Alleviate means to lessen. Eliminate would mean ending it completely, which the passage rules out.

wrong.d: Eliminate means to remove entirely, but the passage says the crisis did not end.
wrong.a: Rice and water would not make hunger worse.

items.prompt: Which word fits best?
items.passage: The new bike lanes will not solve the city's traffic problems, but planners hope they will ___ some of the rush-hour crowding.
items.clue: will not solve; some of
items.hint: The lanes won't fix everything. Which word means to make it partly better?
items.explanation: "Will not solve" and "some of" tell you the lanes should make crowding less bad, not end it. Alleviate fits. Cure is too strong, since it means fixing completely.

wrong.a: Cure means to fix completely; the passage says the lanes won't solve it.
wrong.b: Planners don't want to create crowding.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what alleviate means.

chunks.text: Hana drank three cups of coffee.

items.hint: Which action would make nervousness less severe?
items.explanation: Deep breathing calms nerves, so it alleviates them. Lots of coffee would likely make her jitterier, the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "alleviate" in this sentence?
items.passage: The town built a second bridge to alleviate the pressure on the old one, which was starting to crack.
items.hint: What would a second bridge do to the load on the first?
items.explanation: A second bridge takes some traffic away, easing the pressure on the old one. Ease matches alleviate. Repair would mean fixing the cracks, which a new bridge doesn't do.

wrong.d: The new bridge reduces the load; it doesn't fix the cracks.
wrong.b: Increase is the opposite.

words.definition: chosen or decided without a good reason or fair rule, as if at random

hero.text: The villain's rules were arbitrary: one day hats were banned, the next day shoes, and nobody knew why.

words.everyday: Students complained that the new seating chart felt arbitrary, since the teacher gave no reason for it.

contrast.nonExample: The coach picked the starting team based on who scored best in practice drills.
contrast.explanation: An arbitrary choice has no clear reason. Choosing by practice scores follows a clear, fair rule.

items.prompt: Which decision is arbitrary?

options.text: The library closes at 6 because that is when the last bus leaves.
A class picks a field-trip site by voting.
The manager fires a worker just because he dislikes her shirt color.
The pool closes during lightning for safety.

items.hint: Which decision has no good reason behind it?
items.explanation: Firing someone over a shirt color has no good reason, so it is arbitrary. The other decisions are based on buses, a vote, or safety.

wrong.a: The bus schedule is a real reason.
wrong.d: Safety is a good reason.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In some ancient kingdoms, a ruler could jail anyone for any reason, or for no reason at all. Documents like the Magna Carta tried to protect people from this kind of ___ punishment.
items.clue: for any reason, or for no reason at all
items.hint: What do you call punishment given for no reason?
items.explanation: "For no reason at all" is the defining clue. Punishment without a fair reason or rule is arbitrary. Lawful would mean following rules, the opposite.

wrong.d: Lawful punishment follows rules; this had none.
wrong.c: Whether it was public isn't the point of the clue.

items.prompt: Is the teacher's choice arbitrary?
items.passage: Ms. Kato sets the essay length at 500 words because that's how long the state test essay will be.
items.hint: Does she have a reason?
items.explanation: No. Ms. Kato has a clear reason: matching the state test. An arbitrary choice has no real reason behind it.

items.prompt: Which line uses "arbitrary" correctly?

options.text: "The rule is arbitrary because the safety experts tested it for years."
"My arbitrary dog always comes when I call."
"He was so arbitrary that he finished his homework early."
"Why must the line form on the left? That seems totally arbitrary."

items.hint: Which speaker is pointing out a rule with no clear reason?
items.explanation: The speaker can't see any reason for the line rule, so calling it arbitrary fits. A rule tested for years has a strong reason, so it isn't arbitrary.

wrong.a: Years of testing give the rule a reason, so it is not arbitrary.
wrong.b: Arbitrary describes choices or rules, not reliable pets.
wrong.c: Finishing early is about effort, not random choices.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "arbitrary" in this sentence?
items.passage: In the math problem, you may pick an arbitrary number for x; the pattern works no matter which one you choose.
items.clue: no matter which one you choose
items.hint: If any number works, how do you choose it?
items.explanation: In math, arbitrary means any choice at all, picked at random. Unfair doesn't fit here, since nobody is being treated badly by choosing a number.

wrong.c: Arbitrary can suggest unfairness in rules, but in this math sentence it just means any number at all.
wrong.d: Any number works, so there isn't one correct number.

words.definition: to express an idea or feeling clearly in words

hero.text: After the rescue, Kai struggled to articulate how scared he had been, but finally he found the right words.

words.everyday: In her essay, Zoe articulated three clear reasons the school should start later.

contrast.nonExample: Asked why he liked the book, Max just shrugged and said, "I dunno, it was good."
contrast.explanation: To articulate an idea is to put it into clear words. A shrug and "I dunno" do not express a reason clearly.

items.prompt: What does "articulate" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Before the debate, Nadia practiced articulating her main argument in just two sentences.
items.hint: Why would she practice saying it in just two sentences?
items.explanation: Nadia is practicing putting her argument into clear, short words. That is what articulate means.

wrong.b: Nothing suggests anger.
wrong.a: Memorizing is different from expressing an idea clearly.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Jonah knew the painting made him feel something, but he couldn't ___ what. After staring at it for ten minutes, he finally wrote, "It feels lonely, like the last day of summer."
items.clue: finally wrote, "It feels lonely…"
items.hint: He had the feeling already. What was hard was putting it into…
items.explanation: Jonah had the feeling but struggled to put it into words, then finally wrote it down. Articulate means to express clearly in words. Imagine doesn't fit, because the feeling was already there.

wrong.b: He already felt it; the struggle was finding words.
wrong.d: He was staring for ten minutes, so he wasn't ignoring it.

items.prompt: Did Carmen articulate her concern?
items.passage: At the town meeting, Carmen stood up and said, "The crosswalk near the school has no light, and two kids were almost hit last month. We need a signal there."
items.hint: Did she say clearly what the problem was and what she wanted?
items.explanation: Yes. Carmen named the problem, gave evidence, and said what she wanted, all in clear words. That is articulating a concern.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what articulate means.

chunks.text: In his speech, the class president
so clearly that everyone understood them.
so quietly that no one could follow.

items.hint: Articulating means expressing clearly. Which ending matches?
items.explanation: Expressing goals so clearly that everyone understood shows articulating. If no one could follow, the goals weren't expressed clearly.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "articulated" in this sentence?
items.passage: The Declaration of Independence articulated ideas about rights that many colonists already believed but had never seen written so plainly.
items.clue: already believed but had never seen written so plainly
items.hint: The colonists already believed the ideas. What did the document do with them?
items.explanation: The ideas already existed; the Declaration expressed them clearly in writing. Invented is wrong because the passage says colonists already believed them.

wrong.a: The colonists already believed the ideas, so the document didn't invent them.
wrong.d: The document stated the ideas; it didn't question them.

words.definition: kind and wanting to help or do good for others

hero.text: The benevolent old inventor gave Pixel her best tools for free, saying only, "Use them to help people."

words.everyday: A benevolent neighbor shoveled the walks of every older person on the block after the blizzard.

contrast.nonExample: The landlord raised the rent on his poorest tenants just because he knew they couldn't move.
contrast.explanation: A benevolent person wants good things for others. Taking advantage of people is the opposite.

items.prompt: Bene- means "good" and vol means "wish." A benevolent person most likely…
items.hint: Put "good" and "wish" together.
items.explanation: Bene (good) + vol (wish) = wishing good. A benevolent person wishes good things for others. You see bene in benefit, too.

wrong.c: Getting wishes is luck, not kindness.
wrong.d: Bene means good in the sense of doing good, not skill.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the queen?
items.passage: The young queen lowered taxes during the famine, opened the royal storehouses to hungry families, and built free hospitals. Even her critics admitted she seemed to truly care for her people.
items.clue: opened the royal storehouses; built free hospitals; truly care for her people
items.hint: Polite describes manners. What describes actions that do real good?
items.explanation: Feeding the hungry and building free hospitals show she wanted to do good for others, so benevolent fits. Polite is only about good manners, which is much weaker.

wrong.d: Polite is about manners; her actions go much further than that.
wrong.a: She may be wealthy, but the clues describe her kindness.

items.prompt: Is this an example of a benevolent act?
items.passage: A company donated money to a children's hospital, but only so it could put its logo on the building and sell more products.
items.hint: Look at why the company gave the money.
items.explanation: No. The company's main goal was selling more, not helping others. Benevolent describes a real wish to do good, not giving for advertising.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In the novel, everyone fears the old hermit on the hill. At the end, readers learn he has secretly been leaving food on the doorsteps of poor families for years. He was ___ all along.
items.clue: secretly been leaving food on the doorsteps of poor families
items.hint: What does leaving food for poor families show about him?
items.explanation: Secretly feeding poor families shows a kind wish to help, so he was benevolent. He might be lonely or mysterious, but the clue is about his kindness.

wrong.c: He seemed mysterious, but the ending reveals kindness.
wrong.a: The ending shows the fear was wrong.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "benevolent" in this sentence?
items.passage: The fairy tale's benevolent godmother helps the girl escape, while her stepmother plots against her.
items.hint: Think of the stepmother, who plots against the girl.
items.explanation: Malicious means wanting to cause harm, the opposite of benevolent, which means wanting to do good. Magical and elderly describe the godmother but are not opposites.

wrong.b: Magical isn't about kindness at all.
wrong.d: Shy is about confidence, not kindness.

words.definition: honest and direct, even when the truth is uncomfortable

hero.text: Rex was candid with the team: "My plan failed, and it was my fault."

words.everyday: Lucia asked for a candid opinion of her poem, so her friend told her the ending felt rushed.

contrast.nonExample: When asked if he'd broken the vase, Owen changed the subject and talked about the weather.
contrast.explanation: A candid person speaks openly and honestly. Dodging the question is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which response is the most candid?
items.passage: A friend asks, "Did you like my band's concert?" You thought the songs were great but the sound was too loud.

options.text: "The songs were great, but honestly, the sound was way too loud."

items.hint: Which answer is honest and direct about both the good and the bad?
items.explanation: Candid means honest and direct. This answer shares the real opinion, including the uncomfortable part about the sound.

wrong.a: "Perfect" isn't honest, since you thought the sound was too loud.
wrong.b: Changing the subject avoids the question.
wrong.d: Refusing to answer is guarded, not candid.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the coach's feedback?
items.passage: "You have real talent," the coach told Asha, "but you skip drills, and right now that's why you're on the bench." It stung, but Asha appreciated that he didn't sugarcoat it.
items.clue: didn't sugarcoat it; appreciated
items.hint: The feedback was honest and direct, but was it meant to hurt?
items.explanation: The coach was honest and direct without trying to be mean, and Asha appreciated it. That is candid. Rude would mean disrespectful, but he also praised her talent.

wrong.a: Rude suggests disrespect, but the coach was fair and Asha appreciated it.
wrong.c: His feedback was specific, not vague.
wrong.d: Flattering would hide the hard truth.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In her memoir, the scientist is surprisingly ___ about her failures. She describes experiments that went wrong, grants she was denied, and a mistake that cost her lab a year of work.
items.clue: describes experiments that went wrong, grants she was denied, and a mistake
items.hint: She openly describes her failures. What word fits that kind of honesty?
items.explanation: She openly shares her failures instead of hiding them, so she is candid. Secretive is the opposite, and boastful would mean bragging about successes.

wrong.a: She shares her failures openly, the opposite of secretive.
wrong.b: Boastful people brag; she admits mistakes.

items.prompt: Which line uses "candid" correctly?

options.text: "Let me be candid: I don't think we can finish the project by Friday."
"He was so candid that he lied about his grades."
"She stayed candid by hiding her real feelings."

items.hint: Look for a speaker about to share an honest, maybe unwelcome, truth.
items.explanation: "Let me be candid" introduces an honest, direct statement that may be unwelcome. Lying or hiding feelings is the opposite of candid.

wrong.b: Lying is the opposite of candid.
wrong.c: Candid describes people or statements, not taste (candied, with an e, means coated in sugar).
wrong.d: Hiding feelings is guarded, not candid.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "candid" in this sentence?
items.passage: In a candid interview, the retired player admitted that he had often been jealous of his teammates.
items.clue: admitted that he had often been jealous
items.hint: He admitted something embarrassing. What kind of interview is that?
items.explanation: Frank means openly honest, like candid. Admitting jealousy is an honest, uncomfortable truth. Private describes who hears it, not how honest it is.

wrong.c: Private is about audience, not honesty.
wrong.a: Length has nothing to do with honesty.

words.definition: something that causes an important change or makes it happen faster

hero.text: Bolt's speech was the catalyst that finally got the whole city to start recycling.

words.everyday: In chemistry class, the enzyme acted as a catalyst, making the reaction happen much faster.

contrast.nonExample: The town's population stayed the same for fifty years, and nothing much changed.
contrast.explanation: A catalyst sparks or speeds up change. When nothing changes, there is no catalyst.

items.prompt: What does "catalyst" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: A single viral video was the catalyst for a nationwide campaign to clean up beaches.

options.text: a problem that cannot be solved

items.hint: What did the video lead to?
items.explanation: The video started a big campaign. A catalyst is something that sparks or speeds up a change.

wrong.b: A catalyst is the thing that causes change, not a video maker.
wrong.c: The video helped start a solution, not a problem.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: For years, people had complained about unsafe factories, but little was done. Then the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire killed 146 workers, and the disaster became the ___ for new safety laws.
items.clue: little was done. Then…; new safety laws
items.hint: The fire led to change after years of nothing happening.
items.explanation: "Little was done" until the fire, and then new laws followed. The fire sparked the change, so it was a catalyst. A barrier would block change.

wrong.a: A barrier blocks change; the fire caused it.
wrong.b: It may be remembered, but the clue is that it caused new laws.

items.prompt: Is the new coach a catalyst?
items.passage: The team had lost every game for two seasons. After a new coach arrived and changed the practice schedule, the team won the championship that same year.
items.hint: Did the coach's arrival spark a big change?
items.explanation: Yes. The coach's arrival sparked a dramatic change, from losing every game to winning the championship. That makes the coach a catalyst.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what catalyst means.

chunks.text: Reading one book about sea turtles
for Mira's career in marine biology.
that changed nothing about Mira's life.

items.hint: A catalyst leads to change. Which ending shows that?
items.explanation: The book sparked a whole career, so it was a catalyst. Something that changes nothing can't be a catalyst.

items.prompt: In this passage, what role does the arrest play?
items.passage: Rosa Parks was not the first person to refuse to give up a bus seat, but her arrest in 1955 helped launch the Montgomery bus boycott, which lasted more than a year and drew national attention to civil rights.

options.text: It was a punishment that ended the movement.
It was a catalyst for a larger protest.
It was a mistake that no one noticed.
It was a result of the boycott.

items.clue: helped launch the Montgomery bus boycott
items.hint: Did the arrest come before or after the boycott? What did it lead to?
items.explanation: "Helped launch" shows the arrest sparked the boycott. Something that sets off a bigger change is a catalyst. It came before the boycott, so it wasn't a result.

wrong.d: The arrest came first and launched the boycott, so it was a cause, not a result.
wrong.a: The movement grew afterward rather than ending.
wrong.c: It drew national attention.

words.definition: to happen at the same time, or to match or agree

hero.text: Nova's training mission coincided with the solar eclipse, so the sky went dark right in the middle of it.

words.everyday: This year, my birthday coincides with Thanksgiving, so we're having pie instead of cake.

contrast.nonExample: The science fair was in March, and the art show was in June.
contrast.explanation: To coincide, two things must happen at the same time (or match). Events months apart do not coincide.

items.prompt: Do the two events coincide?
items.passage: The school play and the big soccer final were both scheduled for Saturday at 2:00, so Leo had to choose one.
items.hint: Are they happening at the same time?
items.explanation: Yes. Both events are on Saturday at 2:00, so they coincide, which is why Leo has to choose.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Many ancient festivals were planned to ___ with the longest day of the year. People gathered to celebrate on the summer solstice itself.
items.clue: on the summer solstice itself
items.hint: The festival happened on the very same day as the solstice.
items.explanation: "On the summer solstice itself" shows the festivals happened at the same time as the longest day. Coincide means to happen at the same time.

wrong.a: Festivals don't compete with a day; they were timed to match it.
wrong.c: Interfere would mean getting in the way.

items.prompt: What does "coincide" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The witness's story coincides with the security footage in every detail.
items.clue: in every detail
items.hint: Coincide can be about time, but here it compares a story and a video.
items.explanation: Here coincide means agree or match: the story and the footage line up "in every detail." This is coincide's matching meaning, not its timing meaning.

wrong.b: Argues with is the opposite of matching.
wrong.a: The sentence is comparing details, not times.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what coincide means.

chunks.text: hundreds of families stopped to buy treats.
it was held a month after everyone left.

items.hint: Coinciding events happen at the same time. Which ending shows why that mattered?
items.explanation: Since the sale happened at the same time as parents' night, many families were there to buy. A month later would not coincide.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
items.passage: Scientists noticed that the frogs' egg-laying ___ with the first heavy spring rains, year after year.
items.clue: year after year
items.hint: These words sound alike. Which one means "happened at the same time"?
items.explanation: Coincided means happened at the same time, so the egg-laying lined up with the rains. Collided means crashed into, and conflicted means clashed, both of which suggest a problem.

wrong.b: Collided means crashed together, which doesn't fit eggs and rain.
wrong.d: Conflicted suggests the two clashed; the timing actually matched.

words.definition: to admit, often unwillingly, that something is true or that you have lost

hero.text: After seeing Pixel's data, Rex conceded that her plan was better than his.

words.everyday: The losing candidate conceded the election and congratulated the winner.

contrast.nonExample: Even after the replay clearly showed the ball was out, Tomas kept insisting it was in.
contrast.explanation: To concede is to admit something is true. Refusing to admit it, even with proof, is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which person concedes?

options.text: Beth refuses to talk about the argument.
Kofi keeps repeating that he is right.
Lily says, "Okay, you have a point. Homework does help me practice."
Sam changes the subject to lunch.

items.hint: Who admits that the other side is partly right?
items.explanation: Lily admits the other person has a point. To concede is to admit something is true, often after arguing against it.

wrong.b: Kofi insists, which is the opposite of conceding.
wrong.a: Refusing to talk is avoiding, not admitting.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Ms. Ruiz argued that the town didn't need a new library. But after seeing that the old one turned away hundreds of visitors each month, she ___ that more space might be necessary.
items.clue: argued … But after seeing
items.hint: She changed her position after seeing evidence. What did she do?
items.explanation: "But after seeing" shows Ms. Ruiz admitting something she had argued against. That is conceding. Demanded is too strong; she only admits it "might be" necessary.

wrong.a: Denied is the opposite; she now accepts the point.
wrong.d: Demanded is too forceful for someone just admitting a point.

items.prompt: Which line uses "concede" correctly?

options.text: "I concede that you're the best, so I'll never admit it."
"Please concede the cookies onto the plate."
"I'll concede the game when I'm ahead by ten points."
"I'll concede that your idea is cheaper, but mine is safer."

items.hint: Conceding means admitting a point. Which speaker admits something?
items.explanation: The speaker admits the other idea is cheaper while still arguing for safety. Conceding a point in an argument often sounds like this.

wrong.a: Conceding is admitting, so "never admit it" contradicts itself.
wrong.b: Concede isn't about placing objects.
wrong.c: People concede when losing, not when ahead.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "conceded" in this sentence?
items.passage: The scientist conceded that her first experiment had a flaw, and she redesigned it.
items.hint: She owned up to the flaw.
items.explanation: Admitted matches conceded. Discovered is close, but conceding means accepting something, often reluctantly, not just finding it.

wrong.c: Discovering is finding; conceding is admitting.
wrong.b: Hid is the opposite.

items.prompt: What does "concede" mean in this passage?
items.passage: Down by forty points with two minutes left, the chess club's opponents finally laid down their king. They chose to concede rather than play out a game they could not win.
items.clue: laid down their king; could not win
items.hint: Why would a player lay down the king before the game is over?
items.explanation: Laying down the king and giving up a game you can't win means admitting defeat. That's conceding a game.

wrong.d: They ended the game, not paused it.
wrong.a: Nothing suggests cheating.

words.definition: general agreement among most or all members of a group

hero.text: After an hour of debate, the heroes reached a consensus: they would protect the bridge first.

words.everyday: There is a strong scientific consensus that regular exercise improves health.

contrast.nonExample: The class split into three groups, each insisting on a different field-trip destination.
contrast.explanation: A consensus means the group mostly agrees. A class split three ways has no consensus.

items.prompt: Did the group reach a consensus?
items.passage: The student council voted 4 to 4 on the new dress code, and members left the meeting still arguing.
items.hint: Does the group mostly agree?
items.explanation: No. A tie vote and continued arguing show the group is split. A consensus means general agreement among most or all members.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Hundreds of climate researchers from different countries studied the data independently. Nearly all of them came to the same conclusion, creating a strong ___ about the cause of rising temperatures.
items.clue: Nearly all of them came to the same conclusion
items.hint: What do you call it when nearly everyone agrees?
items.explanation: "Nearly all of them came to the same conclusion" describes general agreement, a consensus. A debate would mean they disagreed.

wrong.b: A debate means disagreement; these researchers agreed.
wrong.a: A rumor is unconfirmed talk, not careful research.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the result?
items.passage: Out of thirty students, twenty-eight wanted to donate the bake-sale money to the animal shelter. The other two said they didn't mind.
items.clue: twenty-eight wanted; the other two didn't mind
items.hint: Nobody gave anything up; nearly everyone just agreed.
items.explanation: Almost everyone agreed and no one objected, so there was a consensus. A compromise happens when each side gives something up, which didn't happen here.

wrong.c: A compromise means both sides give something up; here people simply agreed.
wrong.b: No one argued.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what consensus means.

chunks.text: when all five members chose "Static Sky."
when each member chose a different name.

items.hint: A consensus needs agreement. Which ending shows everyone agreeing?
items.explanation: All five members choosing the same name is a consensus. Each choosing a different name shows no agreement at all.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "consensus" in this sentence?
items.passage: Historians have no consensus about why the ancient city was abandoned; some blame drought, others war, others disease.
items.hint: The historians offer different explanations. What is the opposite of agreeing?
items.explanation: Disagreement is the opposite of consensus. The passage shows historians split among drought, war, and disease. Theory is just one idea, not an opposite.

wrong.c: A theory is a possible explanation, not the opposite of agreement.
wrong.a: Evidence is what historians use; it isn't the opposite of agreement.

words.definition: able to be believed or trusted because of good evidence or reliability

hero.text: Juniper only trusted credible sources, so she checked the weather service before warning the city about the storm.

words.everyday: For her report, Anya used credible sources like encyclopedias and science journals, not random blogs.

contrast.nonExample: A website with no author, lots of spelling errors, and wild claims about "miracle cures."
contrast.explanation: A credible source has good reasons to be trusted. A site with no author and wild claims gives you no reason to trust it.

items.prompt: The root cred means "believe," and -ible means "able to be." Credible most likely means…
items.hint: Put the two parts together.
items.explanation: Cred (believe) + -ible (able to be) = able to be believed. The same root appears in credit and incredible (not believable).

wrong.a: That links to credit cards, but cred means believe.
wrong.d: Incredible can mean surprising, but credible means believable.

items.prompt: Which source is the most credible for a report on volcanoes?

options.text: a video by an anonymous user titled "Volcano SECRETS They Don't Want You to Know"
a comment on a gaming forum
a report from a national geological survey
a friend's older brother who visited Hawaii once

items.hint: Which source has experts and evidence behind it?
items.explanation: A national geological survey is run by scientists who study volcanoes, so it is credible. An anonymous video with a dramatic title gives no reason to trust it.

wrong.a: An anonymous source with a sensational title is not trustworthy.
wrong.d: Visiting once doesn't make someone an expert.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The jury did not believe the first witness, who had changed his story three times. The second witness, however, was ___: her account matched the phone records and two other people's statements.
items.clue: matched the phone records and two other people's statements
items.hint: Her story was backed by other evidence. What does that make her?
items.explanation: Her account matched other evidence, so she could be believed: credible. The contrast word "however" separates her from the first witness, who wasn't believed.

wrong.c: Her story matched the records, so she was not mistaken.
wrong.a: Nothing describes her feelings.

items.prompt: Is this a credible claim?
items.passage: A toothpaste ad says, "Dentists recommend us!" but doesn't name any dentists, studies, or sources.
items.hint: Is there any evidence that makes the claim trustworthy?
items.explanation: No. The ad gives no names, studies, or sources, so there is no good reason to believe it. A credible claim is backed by evidence or a reliable source.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "credible" in this sentence?
items.passage: Because she had studied wolves in the wild for twenty years, the biologist was a credible voice in the debate over reintroducing them.
items.clue: studied wolves in the wild for twenty years
items.hint: Why would twenty years of study matter?
items.explanation: Her long experience gives people reason to believe her, so she is trustworthy. Popular means liked by many, which is different from being believable.

wrong.b: Being liked is not the same as being believable.
wrong.a: Loudness doesn't make someone trustworthy.

words.definition: lacking something that is needed; not having enough

hero.text: The robot's battery was deficient in power, so Bolt had to recharge it before the race.

words.everyday: Plants grown in soil deficient in nitrogen often have yellow leaves.

contrast.nonExample: The garden had plenty of water, sunlight, and rich soil, and the tomatoes grew huge.
contrast.explanation: Deficient means lacking something needed. A garden with everything it needs is not deficient.

items.prompt: What does "deficient" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Sailors long ago often got sick because their diet was deficient in vitamin C.
items.hint: Why would the sailors get sick?
items.explanation: The sailors got sick because they didn't get enough vitamin C. Deficient means lacking something needed.

wrong.a: Full of is the opposite.
wrong.b: Vitamin C doesn't harm people; lacking it does.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The inspectors closed the old bridge. Its steel supports were rusted through, and its safety rails were missing in several places. The bridge was ___ in almost every way that mattered.
items.clue: rusted through; missing in several places
items.hint: The bridge lacked strong supports and rails it needed.
items.explanation: Rusted supports and missing rails show the bridge lacked what it needed to be safe. That's deficient. Efficient sounds similar but means working well without waste.

wrong.d: Efficient sounds similar but means working well, the opposite of this bridge.
wrong.b: It may be old, but the clues describe what it lacks.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "deficient" in this sentence?
items.passage: The report found the school's science equipment deficient, with too few microscopes for each class.
items.hint: The opposite of not having enough is having…
items.explanation: Adequate means enough for what is needed, the opposite of deficient. Broken is a problem too, but it is not the opposite of lacking.

wrong.b: Broken is another kind of problem, not the opposite.
wrong.c: Modern equipment could still be too few in number.

items.prompt: Is the essay deficient?
items.passage: The assignment asked for an introduction, three supporting paragraphs, and a conclusion. Noah's essay had an introduction and one paragraph, then just stopped.
items.hint: Is the essay missing parts it needs?
items.explanation: Yes. The essay is missing two paragraphs and a conclusion, so it lacks required parts. That makes it deficient.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the plan?
items.passage: The city's flood plan looked good on paper, but it had only enough sandbags for half the riverbank and no way to warn people living near the water.
items.clue: only enough sandbags for half; no way to warn people
items.hint: What does the plan not have enough of?
items.explanation: The plan lacks enough sandbags and a warning system, so it is deficient. Nothing suggests it is complicated or costly.

wrong.a: The problem is missing pieces, not complexity.
wrong.d: Cost isn't mentioned.

words.definition: to become worse in condition or quality over time

hero.text: As the storm went on, the weather deteriorated, and Nova had to fly lower to see through the rain.

words.everyday: Without care, old photographs can deteriorate, fading and cracking over the years.

contrast.nonExample: With practice every day, Ava's piano playing got smoother and more confident.
contrast.explanation: To deteriorate is to get worse. Ava's playing is improving, the opposite.

items.prompt: Is the house deteriorating?
items.passage: No one has lived in the old farmhouse for years. The paint is peeling, the roof leaks more each winter, and the porch is starting to sag.
items.hint: Is the house getting worse over time?
items.explanation: Yes. Peeling paint, a roof that leaks "more each winter," and a sagging porch show the house getting worse over time. That is deteriorating.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: At first the two countries traded peacefully. But after a dispute over fishing rights, relations began to ___, and soon each side had closed its embassy.
items.clue: after a dispute; closed its embassy
items.hint: Did things get better or worse after the dispute?
items.explanation: The dispute led to closed embassies, so relations got worse over time. Deteriorate fits. Freeze would mean stopping still, but the passage shows a steady slide.

wrong.a: Closing embassies shows things got worse, not better.
wrong.d: Freeze suggests stopping; the passage shows things sliding downhill.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.passage: The patient's condition did not collapse suddenly; it ___ slowly over several weeks, so doctors had time to try new treatments.
items.clue: did not collapse suddenly; slowly over several weeks
items.hint: Look for a word that means getting worse gradually, not all at once.
items.explanation: Deteriorate means to get worse, often gradually, which matches "slowly over several weeks." Crashed and exploded suggest something sudden, which the sentence rules out.

wrong.a: Crashed means a sudden drop, but the sentence says it was slow.
wrong.d: Recovered means got better.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what deteriorate means.

chunks.text: deteriorated into a shiny new trophy.

items.hint: Deteriorating means getting worse. Which result is worse?
items.explanation: A soggy mess is worse than the original model, so it deteriorated. A shiny new trophy would be an improvement.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "deteriorated" in this sentence?
items.passage: Over centuries, wind and rain deteriorated the ancient statue until its face was barely recognizable.
items.clue: barely recognizable
items.hint: What did wind and rain do to the statue's face?
items.explanation: Wore down means slowly damaged, matching deteriorated. The face became barely recognizable because it got worse over time.

wrong.b: Repaired is the opposite.
wrong.c: Covering wouldn't make the face unrecognizable over centuries.

words.definition: a hard choice between two or more options, often where none is fully good

hero.text: Kai faced a dilemma: rescue the cat on the roof or catch the runaway bus. He couldn't do both at once.

words.everyday: Mina's dilemma was whether to tell the teacher her friend had cheated or stay quiet and keep the friendship.

contrast.nonExample: Jack had to decide between a free ice cream and nothing, so he took the ice cream.
contrast.explanation: A dilemma is a difficult choice. Choosing between free ice cream and nothing is easy.

items.prompt: Which person faces a dilemma?

options.text: Raj picks a red pen because it's the only one left.
Tess finishes her chores and goes outside.
Uma's two best friends are having parties on the same night, and she'll hurt one of them no matter which she picks.

items.hint: Look for a hard choice where every option has a downside.
items.explanation: Uma must choose, and both choices hurt a friend. A hard choice with no fully good option is a dilemma.

wrong.a: With only one pen, there is no real choice.
wrong.d: Following a habit isn't a hard choice.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The town council faced its toughest ___ yet. Building the new factory would bring hundreds of jobs, but it would also pollute the river where families fished and swam.
items.clue: would bring hundreds of jobs, but it would also pollute
items.hint: Both choices have a cost. What do you call that kind of decision?
items.explanation: Jobs versus a clean river is a hard choice with real downsides either way. That is a dilemma.

wrong.c: Nothing has been won yet; they still have to choose.
wrong.a: A hard choice is not a celebration.

items.prompt: Is this a dilemma?
items.passage: Lucas has a test tomorrow. He can study tonight or play video games. He knows studying is right, and he doesn't really mind giving up the game.
items.hint: Is this choice actually hard for Lucas?
items.explanation: No. Lucas already knows what to do and doesn't mind the cost, so the choice isn't hard. A dilemma is a difficult choice where each option has a real downside.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the doctor's situation?
items.passage: The doctor had one dose of medicine left and two patients who both needed it to survive.
items.hint: A puzzle has a right answer. Does this situation have one?
items.explanation: Choosing between two patients who both need the medicine is a painful choice with no fully good option, a dilemma. A puzzle has a clear solution once you figure it out.

wrong.a: A puzzle has a solution to find; a dilemma forces a hard trade-off.
wrong.b: The doctor hasn't done anything wrong.
wrong.c: A chore is routine work, not a painful choice.

items.prompt: What is the main character's dilemma in this story summary?
items.passage: In the novel, Elena finds a wallet full of cash just as her family is about to lose their apartment. The owner's ID is inside.

options.text: whether to keep the money her family needs or return it to its owner
how to find a new apartment
what to buy with the cash

items.clue: about to lose their apartment; The owner's ID is inside
items.hint: What two choices pull Elena in different directions?
items.explanation: Elena's family needs money, but she knows whose wallet it is. Keeping it or returning it is the hard choice, her dilemma.

wrong.c: That assumes she keeps it; the dilemma is whether to.
wrong.b: That is a problem, but not the choice the wallet creates.

words.definition: a difference between things that should match

hero.text: Pixel spotted a discrepancy: the map showed four exits, but the building had only three.

words.everyday: The cashier noticed a discrepancy between the price on the shelf and the price on the receipt.

contrast.nonExample: The recipe said two cups of flour, and Ben measured exactly two cups.
contrast.explanation: A discrepancy is a mismatch. When the amounts match, there is no discrepancy.

items.prompt: Is there a discrepancy?
items.passage: The class roster lists 24 students, but when the teacher counts heads, only 22 are in the room and no one is absent.
items.hint: Do the two numbers match?
items.explanation: Yes. The roster says 24 but the count is 22, with no one absent. Two things that should match don't, so there is a discrepancy.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The suspect said he left the party at 9:00, but the doorbell camera showed him leaving at 11:30. Detectives wanted to know the reason for the ___.
items.clue: said he left … at 9:00, but the doorbell camera showed … 11:30
items.hint: His story and the video don't match.
items.explanation: The suspect's time and the camera's time are different, but they should match. That difference is a discrepancy.

wrong.a: The times disagree, so it is the opposite of agreement.
wrong.d: A schedule is a plan, not a mismatch.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "discrepancy" in this sentence?
items.passage: Scientists noticed a discrepancy between the predicted and actual orbit of Uranus, which eventually led to the discovery of Neptune.
items.hint: The prediction and the real orbit didn't line up.
items.explanation: A mismatch between prediction and reality is a discrepancy. Distance is a measurement, not a difference between what was expected and what happened.

wrong.b: Distance is how far apart things are, not a mismatch.
wrong.c: Similarity is the opposite.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what discrepancy means.

chunks.text: one showed the river flowing north, the other south.
both showed the river in exactly the same place.

items.hint: A discrepancy is a mismatch. Which ending shows one?
items.explanation: North versus south is a mismatch between maps that should agree, so it's a discrepancy. Maps that match exactly have no discrepancy.

items.prompt: Which detail shows a discrepancy in this account?
items.passage: In his journal, the explorer wrote that he spent the whole winter at the fort. Yet a letter in his handwriting, dated January, was mailed from a town two hundred miles away.

options.text: His letter came from a town far from the fort in winter.
The town was two hundred miles away.
He wrote in his own handwriting.

items.clue: Yet a letter … was mailed from a town two hundred miles away
items.hint: Which detail doesn't match what the journal says?
items.explanation: The journal says he stayed at the fort all winter, but the January letter came from far away. Those two facts don't match, which is a discrepancy.

wrong.c: The distance matters only because it clashes with the journal; alone it is just a fact.
wrong.a: Keeping a journal doesn't conflict with anything.

words.definition: to draw out a response, answer, or reaction from someone

hero.text: Juniper's joke elicited a laugh from even the grumpiest villain in the room.

words.everyday: The teacher's question elicited a lively discussion about whether zoos help animals.

contrast.nonExample: The speaker asked a question, and the audience sat in total silence.
contrast.explanation: To elicit is to draw out a response. If nobody responds, nothing was elicited.

items.prompt: What does "elicit" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The sad ending of the movie elicited tears from almost everyone in the theater.
items.hint: What did the ending cause the audience to do?
items.explanation: The ending brought out tears from the audience. Elicit means to draw out a reaction.

wrong.a: The ending caused tears rather than stopping them.
wrong.b: Tears came out; nothing was hidden.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The reporter asked the mayor the same question three different ways, hoping to ___ a clear answer about where the money had gone.
items.clue: asked … three different ways, hoping to
items.hint: The reporter wanted to get something out of the mayor.
items.explanation: Asking three ways shows the reporter was trying to draw out an answer. Elicit means to draw out a response.

wrong.b: The reporter wanted an answer, not to avoid one.
wrong.d: Erase doesn't fit getting an answer.

items.prompt: These words sound alike. Which one fits?
items.passage: The scientist's surprising results were sure to ___ strong reactions from other researchers.
items.clue: strong reactions
items.hint: Which word means to draw out a reaction?
items.explanation: Elicit means to draw out, so surprising results elicit reactions. Illicit sounds almost the same but is an adjective meaning illegal.

wrong.a: Illicit means illegal; it describes things and isn't an action.
wrong.b: Elect means to choose by voting.
wrong.d: Erect means to build or stand upright.

items.prompt: Which line uses "elicit" correctly?

options.text: "I elicited the box onto the top shelf."
"Her question elicited a long silence, then a nervous laugh."
"Please elicit your shoes at the door."

items.hint: Look for a sentence where something draws out a reaction.
items.explanation: The question drew out a reaction (silence, then a laugh), so it elicited them. Elicit is about drawing out responses, not moving objects.

wrong.a: Elicit isn't about lifting or placing things.
wrong.c: You remove shoes; you don't elicit them.
wrong.d: Elicit is a verb, not a description of cookies.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "elicit" in this sentence?
items.passage: Good interviewers ask open-ended questions to elicit detailed stories, not just yes-or-no answers.
items.hint: What are open-ended questions trying to get from the person?
items.explanation: Open-ended questions bring out longer stories. Bring out matches elicit. Record is what happens after the story is told, not what draws it out.

wrong.c: Recording keeps the answer; eliciting draws it out in the first place.
wrong.a: Prevent is the opposite.

words.definition: to publicly support or approve of a person, plan, or product

hero.text: The academy's teachers endorsed Pixel's plan to build a solar-powered training gym.

words.everyday: The local newspaper endorsed Ms. Okafor for mayor in an editorial on Sunday.

contrast.nonExample: The scientist privately thought the plan was fine but refused to say anything about it in public.
contrast.explanation: To endorse is to support something openly. Keeping quiet about it is not endorsing.

items.prompt: Is the coach endorsing the new rule?
items.passage: At the league meeting, the coach stood up and said, "I fully support the new helmet rule. Every team should follow it."
items.hint: Is the coach openly supporting the rule?
items.explanation: Yes. The coach publicly says he supports the rule. To endorse is to openly approve of something.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Before the vote on the new park, three former mayors wrote a joint letter to the newspaper. They urged residents to vote yes, saying they ___ the plan completely.
items.clue: urged residents to vote yes
items.hint: What were the former mayors doing by urging a yes vote?
items.explanation: Writing a public letter urging a yes vote is public support, which means they endorsed the plan. Nothing says they designed it.

wrong.a: Questioning would mean doubting; they urged a yes vote.
wrong.d: The passage says they supported it, not that they created it.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.passage: The doctor didn't just mildly like the new vaccine schedule; she publicly ___ it on national television.
items.clue: didn't just mildly like; publicly
items.hint: The word must be stronger than "mildly like" and done in public.
items.explanation: Endorsed means publicly supported, which is stronger than mildly liking. Tolerated means put up with, which is weaker.

wrong.b: Tolerated means putting up with something, weaker than mildly liking.
wrong.d: Doubted is the opposite of support.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what endorse means.

chunks.text: by praising them in a TV ad.
by warning fans never to buy them.

items.hint: Endorsing is public support. Which ending shows that?
items.explanation: Praising the sneakers in an ad is public approval, an endorsement. Warning fans against them is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "endorsed" in this sentence?
items.passage: Several environmental groups endorsed the law, praising its limits on factory pollution.
items.hint: What would the groups do if they were against the law?
items.explanation: Opposed means stood against, the opposite of endorsed. Supported is a synonym, not an opposite.

wrong.c: Supported means nearly the same as endorsed.
wrong.a: Studying is neutral; it is neither for nor against.

words.definition: to be a typical or excellent example of something

hero.text: Nova exemplifies courage: she always steps forward first, even when she's afraid.

words.everyday: The Golden Gate Bridge exemplifies the suspension bridge design.

contrast.nonExample: Calling a penguin a typical bird would be strange, since most birds can fly.
contrast.explanation: To exemplify is to be a clear, typical example. A penguin is an unusual bird, so it doesn't exemplify birds in general.

items.prompt: What does "exemplifies" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: With its huge columns and triangular roof, the old courthouse exemplifies Greek-style architecture.
items.hint: The word "example" is hiding inside exemplify.
items.explanation: The courthouse has the columns and roof typical of Greek style, so it is a clear example of it. That's what exemplifies means.

wrong.a: Nothing says it is a bad copy.
wrong.c: Age is not the point; the features are.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The teacher chose Malia's essay to show the class. It had a clear claim, strong evidence, and a thoughtful conclusion. "This essay ___ everything we've been practicing," she said.
items.clue: chose … to show the class; clear claim, strong evidence
items.hint: Why would the teacher show this essay to everyone?
items.explanation: The essay has all the features the class has practiced, so it is an excellent example of them. It exemplifies them.

wrong.a: The essay includes the skills; it doesn't ignore them.
wrong.b: The essay shows the skills rather than questioning them.

items.prompt: Does this example exemplify a mammal?
items.passage: A student is asked to name an animal that exemplifies mammals. She chooses a dog: it is warm-blooded, has fur, and feeds its puppies milk.
items.hint: Does a dog have the typical features of mammals?
items.explanation: Yes. A dog shows all the typical mammal features: warm blood, fur, and milk for its young. It is a clear example, so it exemplifies mammals.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what exemplify means.

chunks.text: Volunteering every weekend at the shelter,
a total lack of interest in helping.

items.hint: What does volunteering every weekend show a clear example of?
items.explanation: Volunteering every weekend is a clear example of community service. It can't exemplify a lack of interest in helping.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains how the character exemplifies loyalty?
items.passage: In the story, Sam follows his friend Frodo on a dangerous journey, carries him when he can't walk, and refuses to leave even when ordered to go home.

options.text: Sam is strong enough to carry someone.
Sam stays by his friend no matter what.

items.clue: follows; carries him; refuses to leave
items.hint: Which choice sums up the loyal pattern in all three actions?
items.explanation: All three actions show Sam sticking with Frodo through everything, so Sam is a clear example of loyalty. The other choices name single details without explaining the loyalty.

wrong.c: He refuses to leave out of loyalty, not because he likes disobeying.
wrong.b: Strength is a detail, not the quality he exemplifies.

words.definition: stated clearly and directly, leaving nothing to guess

hero.text: Bolt's orders were explicit: "Stay on the roof until I signal. Do not come down early."

words.everyday: The recipe gave explicit directions, listing exact amounts and times for every step.

contrast.nonExample: Dad sighed loudly when he saw the messy kitchen but didn't say anything.
contrast.explanation: Explicit means stated directly. A sigh only hints at what Dad wants, which makes it implied, not explicit.

items.prompt: Which instruction is the most explicit?

options.text: "Put your clothes in the hamper and your books on the shelf by 6:00."

items.hint: Which one says exactly what to do, leaving nothing to guess?
items.explanation: This instruction says what to do, where, and by when. That is explicit: clearly and directly stated.

wrong.a: "Do something" is vague.
wrong.d: A hint is not a direct instruction.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of "explicit" in this sentence?
items.passage: The author never says the character is jealous; the feeling is hinted at through her actions instead of being made explicit.
items.clue: never says; hinted at
items.hint: If something is hinted at rather than stated, it is…
items.explanation: Implied means suggested without being stated, the opposite of explicit. Obvious is close to explicit, not opposite.

wrong.d: Obvious leans toward explicit, not away from it.
wrong.c: Detailed can go along with explicit.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The first contract was vague and caused months of arguments. This time, the lawyers made every rule ___, spelling out exactly who would pay for what and when.
items.clue: spelling out exactly who would pay for what and when
items.hint: The first contract was vague. What is the opposite?
items.explanation: "Spelling out exactly" means stating clearly, which is explicit. It contrasts with the vague first contract.

wrong.a: Flexible rules would leave room for arguments.
wrong.b: Mysterious is like vague, the problem they were fixing.

items.prompt: Is the poem's message explicit?
items.passage: The poem describes a bare tree, an empty swing, and a single glove left on a bench. It never says what the speaker feels.
items.hint: Does the poem state the feeling directly?
items.explanation: No. The poem never states the feeling; readers must infer it from images. That makes the message implied, not explicit.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the warning?
items.passage: The sign at the trailhead read: "DANGER. Bridge closed. Do not cross. Rangers will fine anyone found on the bridge."
items.hint: Is anything left for hikers to guess?
items.explanation: The sign says exactly what is wrong, what to do, and what happens if you don't. That is explicit. Subtle means hinted at, the opposite.

wrong.c: Subtle means quietly hinted; this sign is blunt.
wrong.a: The sign is direct, not especially polite.

words.definition: impressively powerful or difficult, enough to inspire fear or respect

hero.text: The storm-maker was a formidable opponent, but Kai had studied every one of her tricks.

words.everyday: Climbing Mount Everest is a formidable challenge, even for experienced mountaineers.

contrast.nonExample: The first level of the video game was so easy that Leo beat it in two minutes.
contrast.explanation: Formidable means impressively strong or hard. An easy level is not formidable.

items.prompt: What does "formidable" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The chess champion was a formidable player who had not lost a game in five years.
items.hint: What does five years without a loss tell you?
items.explanation: Not losing for five years shows the champion is powerful and hard to beat. That is formidable.

wrong.b: A five-year champion is very experienced.
wrong.a: Formidable is about strength, not friendliness.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The ancient city of Constantinople was protected by massive double walls, a deep moat, and the sea on three sides. For centuries, attackers found its defenses ___.
items.clue: massive double walls, a deep moat, and the sea on three sides
items.hint: How would attackers feel facing walls, a moat, and the sea?
items.explanation: Massive walls, a moat, and the sea made the city very hard to attack. Defenses that powerful are formidable.

wrong.b: Flimsy is the opposite of massive.
wrong.d: Double walls and a moat are far from ordinary.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
items.passage: The science project wasn't just a little tricky; with only two days, no materials, and no partner, Ellie faced a truly ___ task.
items.clue: wasn't just a little tricky; truly
items.hint: You need the strongest word for a very hard task.
items.explanation: "Wasn't just a little tricky" and "truly" call for a strong word. Formidable means impressively hard. Challenging fits the idea but is weaker.

wrong.b: Challenging is right in meaning but not as strong as "truly" demands.
wrong.a: Tiring is about energy, not difficulty.

items.prompt: Is the opponent formidable?
items.passage: Our soccer team was nervous about playing the Hawks, but it turned out they had only five players and had never practiced together. We won 9–0.
items.hint: Were the Hawks actually powerful?
items.explanation: No. The Hawks were weak and easy to beat. Formidable describes an opponent that is truly powerful and hard to defeat.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "formidable" in this sentence?
items.passage: Marie Curie faced formidable obstacles, including poverty and a scientific world that rarely accepted women.
items.hint: How hard were poverty and an unwelcoming scientific world to overcome?
items.explanation: Daunting means so hard it could discourage you, close to formidable. Unusual misses the idea of difficulty.

wrong.b: Minor is the opposite.
wrong.c: The obstacles were hard; whether they were unusual isn't the point.

words.definition: to make it harder for something to happen or progress

hero.text: Thick fog hindered the rescue, so Nova used her heat vision to find the stranded hikers.

words.everyday: Heavy snow hindered the delivery trucks, and many packages arrived days late.

contrast.nonExample: A strong tailwind pushed the runners along, and many set personal records.
contrast.explanation: To hinder is to get in the way. A tailwind helps runners, the opposite of hindering.

items.prompt: Does the noise hinder Ria's studying?
items.passage: Ria tried to study for her test, but the construction outside was so loud that she kept losing her place.
items.hint: Did the noise make studying harder?
items.explanation: Yes. The noise made Ria lose her place, so it made studying harder. That's hindering.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Early explorers of the Arctic were often ___ by sea ice that trapped their ships for months. Some expeditions never reached their goal at all.
items.clue: trapped their ships for months; never reached their goal
items.hint: Did the ice help or get in the way?
items.explanation: Ice that trapped ships and kept expeditions from their goals got in the way. That is hindered.

wrong.a: Ice that traps ships doesn't guide them.
wrong.b: Being trapped for months wouldn't encourage anyone.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the sentence?
